reason: The security best practices quote states IAM Access Analyzer for S3 alerts when a bucket allows access to anyone on the internet or other AWS accounts, including accounts outside your organization; the claim restates it exactly.

The Access Grants page states permissions by prefix, bucket, or object, read-only/write-only/read-write grants to IAM principals and directly to corporate-directory users or groups, and its context describes mapping users and groups to datasets; the FAQ ties directory identities to (IAM) Identity Center; all displays are verbatim.

The Important box states a server access log destination bucket must use SSE-S3 and that with SSE-KMS default encryption log objects might be encrypted with a key you can't access; the claim matches, including the 'might' hedge as 'may'.

The FAQ answer on data access auditing states a bucket can optionally create access log records for all requests and that customers needing IAM/user identity can alternatively configure CloudTrail Data Events; the claim matches.

Under S3 access points the quote defines access points as named network endpoints with dedicated access policies, attached to a data source such as a general purpose bucket, that simplify managing data access at scale for shared datasets.

The first quote requires both the access point and the underlying bucket (or FSx file system) to permit the request; under Delegating access control the second quote recommends delegating bucket access control to access points for use cases that don't need direct bucket access.

The quotes give the Internet and VPC network origins, state S3 rejects requests to a VPC-origin access point that don't originate from that VPC, and state the origin can only be set at creation and can't be changed; the VpcConfiguration condition is in the context.

The FAQ quote states access point policies are written like a bucket policy with the access point ARN as resource, and that S3 evaluates user, bucket, access point, VPC endpoint, SCP and ACL policies to authorize the request.
The Important box states access point policy restrictions apply only to requests made through that access point and attaching an access point does not change the underlying resource's behavior.

The quote states you must modify the VPC endpoint policy to use an access point with a VPC, and requests only succeed through an access point if the endpoint policy grants access to both the access point and the underlying bucket.

The claim says each access point has its own Block Public Access settings, but the quote limits that to 'each access point attached to a bucket' (access points can also attach to directory buckets and FSx volumes), so the claim drops that condition; the own-policy and VPC-only parts are supported.

The FAQ quote states bucket policies can still limit access to specified VPCs, access points give an easier, auditable way to lock all or a subset of a shared dataset to VPC-only traffic, and an SCP can require network origin 'vpc' for any access point created in the organization.

The Note states access points can only perform operations on objects and not other S3 operations such as deleting buckets or creating Replication configurations; the second quote states an attached access point policy works in conjunction with the bucket policy.

The quotas table row (Name | Default | Adjustable | Description) gives Access Points 'Each Account: 10,000', Adjustable Yes, described as per region in an account; default, scope and adjustability match.

The quote and its context state IAM and bucket policies are the simplest approach for small-to-medium dataset counts within the 20 KB bucket policy and 5 KB IAM policy limits, and that access points give significantly more policy space with thousands per Region per account and a policy up to 20 KB each.

Under Account regional namespace general purpose buckets the quote states only your account can create general purpose buckets in this namespace and these buckets can never be re-created by another account.

The ACL overview quotes state each bucket and object has an ACL subresource defining which accounts or groups get which type of access, and that S3 creates a default ACL granting the resource owner full control when a bucket or object is created.
The Important box states that with Bucket owner enforced you must use policies, requests to set or update ACLs fail with AccessControlListNotSupported, and requests to read ACLs are still supported.
The quote states a majority of modern use cases no longer require ACLs and AWS recommends keeping ACLs disabled except where you need to control access for each object individually.

Under Restoring large datasets the quote states requests above the rate are throttled or rejected with ThrottlingException and that Batch Operations can retrieve many objects with a single request, fully utilizing the account's restore request rate.

The storage class quotes state Glacier Instant Retrieval is for rarely accessed long-term data with millisecond retrieval and real-time access, Flexible Retrieval and Deep Archive are archived and not available for real-time access, and the Glacier classes require minimum storage durations and retrieval fees.

The quote says minimum durations and retrieval fees make these classes 'most effective for rarely accessed data'; the claim's 'pay off only for rarely accessed data' adds an exclusive 'only' the quote does not state. The rest (low-cost long-term, minimum durations, retrieval fees) is supported.

Under Cost considerations the quotes state 40 KB total overhead per archived object: 8 KB for name and metadata at S3 Standard rates (for real-time listing) and 32 KB of index metadata at the Glacier class rate (needed to identify and restore); the claim matches.

The quotes state the minimal storage duration is 90 days for Glacier Flexible Retrieval and 180 days for Deep Archive, and deleting or overwriting an archived object within it incurs a prorated early deletion fee.
The Note states objects in S3 Glacier storage classes remain in Amazon S3 and can't be accessed directly through the separate Amazon Glacier service; the claim matches.
Under Restoring archived objects the quote states Amazon S3 processes only one restore request at a time per object.

The quote says provisioned capacity 'helps ensure' Expedited retrieval capacity is available; the claim's 'guarantees' is stronger than the source. The high-demand caveat and the requester-not-bucket-owner purchase are supported verbatim.

Under Provisioned capacity the quote states each unit provides that at least three Expedited retrievals can be performed every 5 minutes and up to 300 MB/s of retrieval throughput, and that without it Expedited retrievals might not be accepted during high demand; the min qualifier covers 'at least'.
The quote states Glacier Instant Retrieval objects are immediately available using GET while Flexible Retrieval and Deep Archive data must first be retrieved with the RestoreObject REST API.

The quote supports 1,000 transactions per second, the ThrottlingException and Batch Operations, with an account-level retrieval-requests quota in context. But the fact marks the rate as not adjustable, which no quote states, and the same section says to contact AWS Support for increased restoration limits.

The claim says you 'pay for both the archive and the temporary copy at the S3 Standard rate', which can be read as both at the Standard rate. The quote bills the archive at the Glacier Flexible Retrieval or Deep Archive rate and only the copy at S3 Standard. 'Number of days' also narrows the quote's 'duration'; the other parts are supported.

The quote states up to 1-2 PB per day per customer account, up to 300 MB/s for objects larger than 5 TB, a 50 TB Flexible Retrieval object taking up to 48 hours, and contacting AWS Support for increased limits; the values and the adjustable condition match.

The quotes name the three options Expedited, Standard and Bulk, state Standard is the default when none is specified, Bulk is the lowest-cost option, and Expedited is a premium feature charged at the Expedited rate; the table row shows Expedited 'Not available' for Deep Archive.

The table row for Glacier Deep Archive or Intelligent-Tiering Deep Archive Access gives Expedited 'Not available', Standard with Batch Operations 9-12 hours, Standard without 'Within 12 hours', and Bulk 'Within 48 hours'; the claim matches cell by cell.

The table row supports 1-5 minutes, 3-5 hours (Minutes-5 hours with Batch Operations) and 5-12 hours. But the same page's prose limits the Expedited 1-5 minutes to objects under 250 MB (larger objects run at up to 300 MB/s) and calls the times typical; the claim states 'takes 1-5 minutes' without that condition.

The example quote states an IAM principal needs permission from both its parent AWS account and the account that owns the resource, and for a bucket operation S3 must verify the bucket owner has granted permission.

The quotes and context support the conversion into one policy set, the user, bucket and object contexts, and the bucket owner's explicit deny. But the claim says all three are evaluated in order and drops the source's conditions: the user context is skipped for root user requests, the object context applies only to object requests, and the explicit-deny check is described for object requests.

The Availability SLA row under its header gives 99.9% for S3 Standard, Express One Zone, Glacier Flexible Retrieval and Deep Archive, and 99% for Intelligent-Tiering, Standard-IA, One Zone-IA and Glacier Instant Retrieval; the footnotes add no SLA condition.

The quotes state AWS Backup creates continuous backups (point-in-time restore) and periodic backups (long-term retention), with restore to a specified point in time in context, and that S3 Versioning must be activated before AWS Backup can back up the bucket.

The storage classes quote states all storage classes except One Zone-IA and Express One Zone are designed to be resilient to the physical loss of an Availability Zone; the Data protection quote lists the same six classes as designed to sustain the loss of an entire AZ.
